messages:
andrew: quick ask — saw a perf regression on the v2 runtime yesterday, small kernel spikes every ~200ms when KV cache misses happen. can someone recommend a minimal nsys smoke flow i can run that will capture the hop without huge traces?

jess: for a quick repro i usually do an nvtx-bracketed short capture: 6-8s is enough to hit a couple of evictions. include trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt so you get both kernel timeline and OSRT markers. keep sampling light.

andrew: perfect — any example CLI?

jess: yep, something like:```bash
nsys profile --output=smoke_v2 --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt --capture-range=nvtx --capture-range-begin="nvtx:trace_start" --capture-range-end="nvtx:trace_end" --duration=7 --sample=none
```

jess: notes: --duration=7 is wallclock cap if bracket fails, --sample=none to avoid huge overhead for this smoke. nvtx begin/end from the process around the workload.

tina: fwiw if you want to see the KV-cache eviction timeline specifically add a short warmup then a single heavy query pattern (seq len + batch churn). osrt helps map thread scheduling/host waits. also try --sample=cpu if you suspect host-side stalls.

andrew: got it. i can add a tiny workload loop to trigger misses. what about file size? last time we blew past quotas.

jess: 7s + sample=none should keep .qdrep < ~40MB usually. if it grows, drop trace to cuda,nvtx only. avoid long-run captures.

ben: if you want kernel hop visibility, open the timeline in Nsight and look for many short device kernels back-to-back (few hundred us). those are usually kernel-launch overheads rather than compute. nvtx categories will show whether it's kvcache path vs batching kernel.

andrew: attached quick paste of the timeline I grabbed earlier (snip):
```
[DEVICE TIMELINE]
0.000s: kernel_batch_step (3.2ms)
0.003s: small_copy_kernel (0.12ms)
0.0032s: kv_lookup_kernel (0.08ms)
0.0033s: tiny_launch_overhead (0.04ms)
0.00334s: kernel_batch_step (2.9ms)
```

tina: that pattern screams frequent small launches (kv_lookup + tiny_copy). try coalescing lookups or use a short prefix cache in host to reduce device hops. also double-check that our kernel selector isn't falling back to an unoptimized kernel for small sequence lengths.

jess: another tip: add NVTX ranges around the batch/kv code so the capture isolates the region you care about. e.g. in C++: ```nvtxRangePushA("kvcache:lookup"); ... nvtxRangePop();``` then use --capture-range=nvtx.

andrew: will run this now. if i paste qdrep somewhere, anyone willing to do a quick look?

perf-bot: automated hint — when posting qdrep, include the nsys CLI you used and the workload seed/args. small captures with NVTX bracket and --sample=none are easiest to triage. :robot_face: 

andrew: thanks all — i'll post the qdrep + CLI shortly. planning one run with trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt and one with trace=cuda,nvtx only to compare sizes.

ben: if you see host-side backlog, run `nsys status` while workload is running to confirm OS-level context switches. also grep for `cudaLaunchKernel` spikes in the timeline view.

jess: last thing — if you need to capture multiple GPUs, add `--capture-range-threads=all` and run short per-GPU hotloops to avoid cross-gpu noise.

andrew: excellent. will update in ~20m.
